title: Email reminders for overdue tasks
subtitle: Tasklet · feature plan

summary.goal: Help users act on overdue tasks without keeping Tasklet open.
changes: Run a scheduled job to detect overdue tasks and avoid duplicate reminders.
Send email reminders with action and unsubscribe links.
Add notification preferences and roll out gradually.
risks: Email delivery depends on domain authentication and relay configuration.
Repeated job runs must never send duplicate reminders.

context:
**Request:** send email reminders for overdue tasks.

Tasklet is a task manager: Express API, SQLite (`better-sqlite3`), framework-free front end in `public/`. About 1,200 active users, **a single instance** in production. Today an overdue task is only shown in red in the list, and only if the user opens the app; no email goes out.

**In scope:** detecting overdue tasks, sending the emails, letting users act or unsubscribe from the email itself. **Out of scope:** push notifications, SMS, per-task reminder settings.

glossary.definition: The standard protocol for sending email: our server hands each message to a relay, which delivers it to the recipients' mailbox providers.
A scheduler that runs a command at fixed times, for example “every 15 minutes”.
The property of an operation that can be replayed with no additional effect: run it twice and it still sends only one email.
DNS records published with the domain that prove to mailbox providers an email really comes from tasklet.app; without them, reminders end up in spam.
Opt-out: on by default, the user can turn it off. Opt-in: off until the user turns it on.
A code appended to a link that only our server can produce: it proves the link comes from one of our emails and hasn't been tampered with.

pages.title: Triggering reminders
pages.intro: What starts the reminders, when a task counts as overdue, and how we make sure the same reminder never goes out twice.

visual.caption: One run of the reminder job, from scheduler to inbox

decisions.title: What triggers the reminders
decisions.benefit: Use a simple scheduler suited to the existing single-instance deployment.
decisions.tradeoff: A scheduler tied to one process needs revisiting if Tasklet scales to several instances.
decisions.why: The trigger decides whether a reminder survives a restart, whether it goes out twice the day we add a second instance, and what extra infrastructure we have to run. Changing it after launch means rewriting how the job is started and monitored.
decisions.proposal: A **cron** inside the Express process (the `node-cron` library) that runs the reminder job every N minutes (D4). Tasklet runs on a single instance: a message queue would be one more service to operate, with nothing to gain today.
decisions.learn_more:
**Why not `setInterval`?** It doesn't align with the clock: a restart at 8:07 shifts every run by 7 minutes. `node-cron` fires at fixed times.

**When to move to a worker?** The day we start a second API instance. The duplicate guard (D3) already prevents duplicate emails, but every instance would repeat the same work.

Docs: [node-cron](https://www.npmjs.com/package/node-cron), [BullMQ](https://docs.bullmq.io/).

facts.label: Open tasks with a due date

options.label: Cron inside the server (node-cron)
options.detail: The job runs in the same process as the API.
pros: Nothing extra to deploy or pay for
Runs the same way in dev and production

A slow run slows down the API

pros: No timer in the code
Isolated from the API: a crash doesn't take it down

Two overdue tasks for the same user produce a single email
A failed send for one user doesn't stop the sends to the next ones

decisions.title: When a task becomes overdue
decisions.why: `due_date` is a date without a time: “September 25” doesn't end at the same instant in Paris and in New York. Get this wrong and the reminder lands in the middle of the night, or flags a task as overdue before it is, and users stop trusting the reminders.
decisions.proposal: A task is overdue **the day after its due date, from 8 am in the user's time zone**. The browser sends its time zone on load; the default is `Europe/Paris`.
decisions.learn_more:
The front end already has this bug: `public/app.js` computes “today” in UTC (`toISOString()`). In New York, after 8 pm, a task due that day already shows as overdue. The “Send the browser's time zone” task fixes it along the way.

Local time is computed in JavaScript (`Intl.DateTimeFormat` with the user's time zone): SQLite knows nothing about time zones.

facts.label: Users outside the Paris time zone

options.label: Per-user time zone
pros: 8 am reminder for everyone, wherever they are
Correct around midnight
cons: A `timezone` column, plus detection in the browser
Local time computed per user in the job

tasks.title: Add the users.timezone column
tasks.do: Migration `003_users_timezone.sql`: `ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN timezone TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Europe/Paris'`. `User.findById` returns `timezone`; `PATCH /api/me` accepts it if it is listed in `Intl.supportedValuesOf('timeZone')`.
acceptance: After `npm run migrate`, existing users have `Europe/Paris`
`PATCH /api/me` with the time zone `Mars/Olympus` returns 400

tasks.title: Send the browser's time zone
tasks.do: In `public/app.js`, after `GET /api/me`, send `Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone` with `PATCH /api/me` if it differs from the stored time zone. Compute `today` in the local time zone instead of UTC.
acceptance: A browser set to America/New_York saves that time zone on first load
No `PATCH` when the stored time zone is already correct
In New York at 9 pm, a task due that day is not shown as overdue

options.label: One time zone for everyone (Europe/Paris)
pros: Nothing to store or detect
A plain SQL query
cons: In New York, the 8 am reminder arrives at 2 am
False overdue flags between midnight and 8 am outside Europe

tasks.title: Overdue tasks query
tasks.do: Add `Task.listOverdue(now)` to `src/models/task.js`: tasks with `done = 0` whose `due_date` is before today's date in the chosen time zone, only once local time is past 8 am. Chosen option: {{choice.label}}. Also return `userId`, `email` and the time zone.
acceptance: At 7:59 am local time, a task due the day before is not returned; at 8:00 am, it is
A task due today, already done or without a due date is never returned

decisions.title: How to guarantee one reminder per task
decisions.why: The job can process the same task twice: a restart mid-run, a manual rerun, a second instance some day. Without a guard, the user gets the same reminder two or three times, and that is the first reason people unsubscribe.
decisions.proposal: Make sending **idempotent**: before sending, the job claims the reminder by inserting `(task_id, kind, period)` into a `reminders` table with a unique key. Insert rejected: the reminder already went out, skip it. Send failed: release the claim, and the next run retries.
decisions.learn_more:
`period` is the due date for a task's reminders, and the ISO week (`2026-W39`) for the Monday digest. If the user pushes the due date back, the period changes and the task can be reminded again.

Why not a simple in-memory set? It is lost on restart, which is exactly the case we need to cover.

The table grows by about 400 rows a day; a daily purge of rows older than 90 days is enough.

visual.caption: The unique key does the work: two concurrent runs can't claim the same row.

options.label: A reminders table with a unique key
pros: The database rejects duplicates, even when two runs overlap
A history of sends, useful for support
cons: One more table and migration
≈ 400 rows a day: needs a purge

tasks.title: Create the reminders table
tasks.do: Migration `002_reminders.sql`: `reminders` table (`id`, `task_id` referencing `tasks(id)` with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, `kind`, `period`, `sent_at` defaulting to `datetime('now')`) with a `UNIQUE (task_id, kind, period)` constraint. `period` is the due date, or the ISO week for the digest.
acceptance: `npm run migrate` creates the table on an existing database without touching tasks
Deleting a task deletes its claims

tasks.title: Reminder model: claim, release, purge
tasks.do: `src/models/reminder.js`: `claim(taskId, kind, period)` runs `INSERT OR IGNORE` and returns `true` if a row was inserted; `release(taskId, kind, period)` deletes it; `purgeOlderThan(days)` deletes older rows.
acceptance: `claim` returns `true`, then `false` for the same triple
`release` followed by `claim` returns `true` again
`purgeOlderThan(90)` leaves today's rows alone

options.label: A last_reminded_at column on tasks
pros: A column instead of a table
Nothing to purge
cons: One reminder per task: no due-day then overdue, no digest
No history for support

tasks.title: Add the tasks.last_reminded_at column
tasks.do: Migration `002_tasks_last_reminded.sql`. `Task.claimReminder(id)` runs `UPDATE tasks SET last_reminded_at = datetime('now') WHERE id = ? AND last_reminded_at IS NULL` and returns `changes === 1`; `Task.releaseReminder(id)` resets the column to `NULL`.
acceptance: Two calls to `claimReminder` on the same task return `true`, then `false`

tasks.title: Claim before sending, release on failure
tasks.do: In `runReminders`, claim each reminder before sending it and skip those already claimed; if the send fails, release the claim so the next run retries. Guard: {{choice.label}}.
acceptance: Two calls to `runReminders` with the same clock send each email only once
After a simulated send failure, the next run sends the reminder again

decisions.title: How often the job runs
decisions.why: The interval sets the maximum delay of a reminder and the load on the database. At 5 minutes, the job queries SQLite 288 times a day, almost always for nothing; at 60 minutes, the 8 am reminder can arrive at 8:59.
decisions.proposal: One run **every 15 minutes**: the reminder arrives between 8:00 and 8:15, for a query that takes a few milliseconds.
decisions.learn_more: Pick a value that divides 60: 5, 10, 15, 20, 30 or 60. With 25, the cron fires at :00, :25 and :50, then again at :00, so once an hour the gap drops to 10 minutes.

tasks.title: One run every {{value}} {{unit}}
tasks.do: Add `REMINDER_INTERVAL_MINUTES` to `src/config.js` (`config.reminders.intervalMinutes`, default {{value}}) and to `.env.example`. Reject a value outside 5–60 at startup.
acceptance: With no environment variable set, `config.reminders.intervalMinutes` is {{value}}
With `REMINDER_INTERVAL_MINUTES=2`, startup fails with a message naming the variable

pages.title: Sending the emails
pages.intro: The service that delivers the emails, how their content is written, and the address they are sent from.

visual.caption: The two ways to send, side by side

decisions.title: Which service sends the emails
decisions.why: This choice decides whether reminders land in the inbox or in spam, and sets the monthly cost. It also dictates the domain setup (SPF, DKIM): switching services means redoing it and rebuilding the sender reputation, which costs several weeks of poorly delivered reminders.
decisions.proposal: Send over **SMTP** with Nodemailer, through the relay of a transactional email provider (Brevo, Postmark or similar). The code depends only on four `SMTP_*` variables: switching providers doesn't touch the code.
decisions.learn_more:
**Ruled out from the start: running our own mail server (Postfix).** Mailbox providers judge an email by the reputation of the IP address that sends it: a new IP lands in spam for weeks, and it is one more server to patch. A provider lends us IPs that are already trusted, for €0–25/month at our volume.

**SMTP or API?** Both go through the same provider. The API also reports bounces and complaints; we can move to it later without changing providers, by replacing only `src/mail/mailer.js`.

Since 2024, Gmail and Yahoo require SPF, DKIM, DMARC and one-click unsubscribe from regular senders: see [Google's guidelines](https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126).

options.label: Provider's SMTP relay (Nodemailer)
options.detail: Nodemailer speaks SMTP to any provider; Mailpit stands in for it locally.
pros: Switch providers by changing 4 variables
Same code in dev and production
cons: Bounces and complaints are only visible in the provider's dashboard
One SMTP connection per run, slower than an HTTP call

acceptance: With `SMTP_HOST` empty in production, startup fails with a message naming the variable
No real values in `.env.example`

options.label: Transactional service's HTTP API
options.detail: HTTP calls to the provider, with a webhook for bounces.
pros: Bounces and complaints reported by webhook
Open and click statistics
cons: Code tied to the provider: switching means rewriting the mailer
One more API key and public route to protect

acceptance: A webhook with an invalid signature returns 401 and changes nothing
After a complaint, the user no longer receives reminders

tasks.title: createMailer sending module

acceptance: `send` returns the message id accepted by the provider
A provider error is surfaced with its code, without the recipient's address in the error message

acceptance: A test email received in Gmail shows `spf=pass` and `dkim=pass` under “Show original”
`nslookup -type=TXT _dmarc.tasklet.app` returns the DMARC record

decisions.title: How to write the email templates
decisions.why: The templates insert task titles typed by users into HTML. A badly escaped title can slip a malicious link into an email sent under Tasklet's name. The choice also sets how long it takes to add a new type of email (D8).
decisions.proposal: JavaScript functions that return `{ subject, text, html }`, with `escapeHtml` applied to all user-supplied data. Every email also has a plain-text version.

options.label: JavaScript functions (template literals)
pros: No dependencies
Testable like any other function
cons: Email HTML written by hand (tables, inline styles)
Escaping relies on discipline: a test enforces it

tasks.title: Templates as JavaScript functions
tasks.do: `src/mail/layout.js`: `layout({ title, body })` produces the shared HTML (600 px table, inline styles) and exports `escapeHtml`. `src/mail/templates.js`: one function per email type, each returning `{ subject, text, html }`.
acceptance: A task titled `` comes out escaped in the HTML
Every template returns a non-empty `text` and a `subject` under 80 characters

options.label: MJML compiled to HTML
pros: Reliable rendering in Outlook as well as Gmail
Readable markup that non-developers can edit
cons: Heavy dependency (≈ 10 MB installed)
Escaping handed off to a template engine (Handlebars)

tasks.title: MJML templates

acceptance: A task titled `` comes out escaped in the HTML
MJML compilation produces no warnings

decisions.title: The address reminders come from
decisions.why: A `noreply` address discourages replies, and user replies need to reach a person.
decisions.proposal: Reminders are sent from `Tasklet <reminders@tasklet.app>`, with `Reply-To: support@tasklet.app`.

pages.title: What users receive
pages.intro: Which emails go out, what users can do straight from an email, and whether reminders are on by default.

visual.caption: The same overdue task, from the user's side

before.title: Today
before.text: The task “Send the quote to Martin”, due yesterday, shows up in red in the list, but only if the user opens Tasklet.

after.title: After
after.text: This morning at 8 am, an email “1 overdue task: Send the quote to Martin”, with a “Mark as done” button and a link to stop these reminders.

decisions.title: Which emails to send
decisions.why: Each type adds a template, a query and more sends. Too many emails and users unsubscribe from everything; too few and overdue tasks go unnoticed, which is the whole point of the request.
decisions.proposal: Three types, to be judged one by one. They go out together: **at most one email per user per day**, with one section per type.

items.title: Due today
items.detail: Tasks due today, so they don't slip. Heads off the delay instead of reporting it after the fact.

tasks.title: “Due today” section
tasks.do: Template: the `dueToday(tasks)` section. In `runReminders`, select tasks due that day (local time ≥ 8 am), claimed with `kind = 'due-today'`.
acceptance: A user with 3 tasks due today receives a single email listing all three
A task checked off before 8 am is not included

items.title: Overdue task
items.detail: The day after the due date, once per task. This is the core of the request.

tasks.title: “Overdue” section
tasks.do: Template: the `overdue(tasks)` section. `runReminders` fills it with the tasks from `Task.listOverdue(now)`, claimed with `kind = 'overdue'` and `period` = the due date.
acceptance: A task due yesterday appears in this morning's email, and never again on the following days
The subject gives the number of tasks: “2 overdue tasks”

items.title: Monday digest
items.detail: On Mondays, every task that has been overdue for more than 7 days. Without it, a forgotten task is reminded only once.

tasks.title: Monday “Still overdue” section
tasks.do: Template: the `weekly(tasks)` section. On Mondays, `runReminders` fills it with tasks overdue for more than 7 days, claimed with `kind = 'weekly'` and `period` = the ISO week.
acceptance: On Monday, a user receives a single email, even if they also have a task that fell overdue the day before
A task overdue for 6 days is not included

tasks.title: One email per user per day
tasks.do: In `runReminders`, group the sections of the selected types by user and send a single `daily({ user, sections })` email (template in `src/mail/templates.js`). The subject reflects the most urgent section; nothing is sent if every section is empty.
acceptance: A user covered by two types receives a single email with two sections
No empty email ever goes out

decisions.title: What users can do from the email
decisions.why: An action button is a link that acts without a sign-in: it must carry a signed token that expires, otherwise anyone could forge the link. Each action is one more public route to secure; with no action at all, users have to open the app, and many won't.
decisions.proposal: A “View task” link and a “Mark as done” button. The button opens a one-click confirmation page, so mail security scanners, which follow links, can't check anything off by mistake.

options.label: “View task” link
pros: No risk: the app asks the user to sign in
cons: A click and a sign-in before acting

tasks.title: Open a task from its link
tasks.do: In `public/app.js`, read `#/tasks/<id>` on load, scroll to the task and highlight it (style in `public/index.html`). The templates add this link to every task.
acceptance: `/#/tasks/42` opens the app with task 42 visible and highlighted
An unknown id shows the list as usual, with no error

options.label: “Mark as done” button
pros: The overdue task is dealt with from the inbox
cons: Public route: signed token, expires after 7 days

tasks.title: “Mark as done” action via signed link
tasks.do: Add the `done` action to `src/routes/links.js`: the `GET` shows the task and a confirmation button, the `POST` calls `Task.markDone`. The template adds the button to every task.
acceptance: Opening the link changes nothing; only the confirmation `POST` marks the task as done
A token altered by one character, or older than 7 days, returns 410 and changes nothing

options.label: “Snooze until tomorrow” button
pros: No follow-up reminder for a task that was simply pushed back
cons: Moves the due date without the user opening the app
One more signed action to maintain

tasks.title: “Snooze until tomorrow” action via signed link
tasks.do: Add the `snooze` action to `src/routes/links.js`: the confirmation `POST` moves `due_date` to the next day, in the user's time zone. The template adds the button.
acceptance: After confirmation, the due date is the next day and no “overdue” reminder goes out that day
A token altered by one character returns 410 and changes nothing

decisions.title: Reminders on by default, or off until enabled
decisions.why: Emailing people who didn't ask for it drives up spam complaints: above a 0.3% complaint rate, Gmail files our mail as spam and the provider (D5) may suspend the account. On the other hand, a setting that is off by default only ever gets turned on by a minority.
decisions.proposal: Reminders **on by default** (opt-out), with a one-click unsubscribe link in every email and a checkbox in the app.
decisions.learn_more:
The unsubscribe link is not optional: Gmail and Yahoo require one-click unsubscribe (`List-Unsubscribe` and `List-Unsubscribe-Post` headers, [RFC 8058](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8058)). That is why it sits in the tasks shared by both options.

The reminders are about the user's own tasks: this is a service email, not marketing. Opt-out is acceptable, as long as unsubscribing is easy.

options.label: On by default, can be turned off (opt-out)
pros: Every user benefits from day one
Nothing to promote in the app
cons: Possibly a few complaints in the first week
One-click unsubscribe is a must

acceptance: After `npm run migrate`, all existing users have `email_reminders = 1`

options.label: Off by default, to be turned on (opt-in)

Those who turn it on read their emails
cons: Low adoption: settings like this are often turned on by fewer than 20% of users
An in-app banner to make it known

Every reminder carries both headers

A user with `email_reminders = 0` no longer receives any reminder

pages.title: Shipping safely
pages.intro: How to test the emails, in what order to ship, and how to open reminders up to users.

visual.caption: Files touched, based on the answers

decisions.title: How to test emails without sending any
decisions.why: Without automated tests, a regression sends wrong reminders to real users, and an email can't be unsent. The choice also sets what a developer has to install to work on the emails.
decisions.proposal: In `npm test`, a test mailer that keeps messages in memory. In development, **Mailpit**: a fake local SMTP server with a web inbox at `localhost:8025`.

options.label: In-memory mailer, plus Mailpit in dev
pros: Fast tests with no network
Real rendering visible locally before production
cons: Mailpit to install (a single binary or Docker)

tasks.title: Mailpit for development
tasks.do: Document `SMTP_HOST=localhost` and `SMTP_PORT=1025` in `.env.example`; add an `npm run mail:dev` script that starts `mailpit`.
acceptance: With Mailpit running, an email sent in dev shows up at http://localhost:8025

options.label: In-memory mailer only
pros: Nothing to install
cons: The HTML rendering is only seen in production

options.label: Provider's sandbox
pros: The real path, headers and DKIM included
cons: Network access and an API key needed in CI
Slow tests, sometimes flaky

tasks.title: Integration test against the sandbox
tasks.do: `test/integration/mail.sandbox.test.js` sends a reminder to the provider's sandbox and checks through the API that it arrived; skipped when `MAIL_SANDBOX_KEY` is not set.
acceptance: Without `MAIL_SANDBOX_KEY`, the test is skipped and `npm test` passes offline

tasks.title: In-memory test mailer
tasks.do: `test/helpers/mailer.js`: `createTestMailer()` has the same interface as `createMailer` and keeps messages in `sent`. The job and template tests use it.
acceptance: No test connects to an SMTP server: `npm test` passes offline
`sent` holds the `to`, `subject`, `text`, `html` and headers of each message

decisions.title: What order to ship in
decisions.why: The order decides what can be shown early and what has to wait. Scheduling before sending lets us measure real volumes without sending anything; sending first lets us test deliverability sooner.
decisions.proposal: Data, then sending, then scheduling, then rollout. Each phase can be tested on its own, and no email reaches a user before the last one.

decisions.title: How to open reminders up to users
decisions.why: An email can't be unsent: a duplicate or a wrong time zone hits everyone who received it. Starting with a small group limits the damage of a bug and gives us a week of real numbers before opening up to everyone.
decisions.proposal: A `REMINDERS_ENABLED` flag, off by default, and a list of 50 pilot users (the team and volunteers) for one week. Then everyone, by emptying the list.

risks.label: Duplicate reminder sent
risks.mitigation: Unique-key claim (D3) and a double-run test

risks.label: Reminders flagged as spam
risks.mitigation: SPF, DKIM and DMARC (D5), one-click unsubscribe (D10)

risks.label: Reminder at the wrong time
risks.mitigation: Per-user time zone (D2), pilots across several time zones

risks.label: SMTP relay down
risks.mitigation: Claim released: the next run retries (D3)

risks.label: Task title injected into the HTML

options.label: Flag and 50 pilots, then everyone
pros: A bug only affects 50 people
A week of real numbers before opening up
cons: One more week before everyone benefits
A pilot list to maintain

tasks.title: Pilot user list
tasks.do: `REMINDERS_PILOT_USER_IDS` (comma-separated ids) in `src/config.js` and `.env.example`. While the list is not empty, `runReminders` skips every other user.
acceptance: With `REMINDERS_PILOT_USER_IDS=1,2`, only users 1 and 2 receive reminders
Empty list: every user who hasn't turned reminders off receives them

options.label: Flag, then everyone at once
pros: Everyone benefits on release day
Nothing to keep up to date
cons: A bug hits 1,200 people at once

tasks.title: REMINDERS_ENABLED flag
tasks.do: `config.reminders.enabled` is `true` only if `REMINDERS_ENABLED=true`: off by default, including in production. Document it in `.env.example`.
acceptance: With no variable set, no run is scheduled
Setting the variable to `false` and restarting stops all sending

decisions.title: What the job writes to the logs
decisions.why: Without a trace, there is no way to answer “I didn't get my reminder”; with too much detail, the logs fill up with email addresses.
decisions.proposal: One JSON line per run (`examined`, `sent`, `failed`, duration) and one line per failure with the task id and the error code, never the email address.

tasks.title: Log a summary of each run
tasks.do: At the end of `runReminders`, write `console.info(JSON.stringify({ event: 'reminders.run', examined, sent, failed, ms }))`; for each failure, a `{ event: 'reminders.failed', taskId, code }` line.
acceptance: Each run writes exactly one `reminders.run` line
No log line contains the `@` character
